alignment.note: Greek καὶ λέγει splits the conjunction and verb into two tokens, while the Peshitta synthetic form ܘܐܡܪ fuses the waw-conjunction with the verb of speaking; the Vulgate likewise separates Et from ait. The grouping here treats the connective with its respective verb across the differing morphological packagings.

Greek uses the historic present λέγει ('he says', present indicative), preserving Mark's vivid narrative tense, whereas the Vulgate renders it with the present/perfect ait and the Peshitta with the perfect ܐܡܪ; both versions normalise the Markan historic present into a past-narrative form.
Greek τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ with article corresponds to Peshitta ܠܗܘ ܓܒܪܐ (preposition + demonstrative + noun) and Latin dative homini.

Greek employs an articular attributive participle phrase (τῷ τὴν ξηρὰν χεῖρα ἔχοντι, 'the one having the withered hand') and the Vulgate matches with a participial habenti manum aridam; the Peshitta restructures the clause as a relative with the predicate fronted (ܕܝܒܝܫܐ ܐܝܕܗ, 'whose hand was withered'), a syntactically distinct but semantically equivalent rendering.

Greek ἔγειρε ('arise/get up') is rendered by the Vulgate with the cognate motion verb Surge, while the Peshitta uses ܩܘܡ (root q-w-m, 'stand up'); all three convey the command to rise, differing only in the lexical nuance between rising and standing.
Greek εἰς τὸ μέσον and Latin in medium correspond to the single Syriac prepositional form ܒܡܨܥܬܐ ('into the midst').

The Vulgate marks the boundary between the narrative frame and the direct speech with an explicit colon (:), a punctuation feature absent from the unpointed Peshitta token stream; the Greek carries the corresponding raised point on ἔχοντι· which is grouped with that participle.
